title: From Self-Taught Beginner to Steam: How Would You Approach This?
author: Embarrassed-Ad-4740
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I'm starting to get into game development as a completely self-taught beginner, and I'm trying to understand both the technical side and the overall process of creating and publishing a game.

My long-term goal is to release a game on **Steam**, but right now I have very little idea about all the steps required to get there. How would you approach it if you were starting today?

The game I'm trying to build is a mix of a **management game**, **RimWorld**, and a **city builder**, focused on resource management, progression, and base/city development.

I'd love to get some advice from people with more experience:

* What would be the main development steps you'd follow for a project like this?
* Which game engine and software would you recommend today?
* Would you start with a very small prototype first, or jump directly into building the full game?
* What are the biggest mistakes beginners should avoid?

To be completely honest, I'm not a professional programmer. I'm trying to build everything with the help of modern AI tools, which can often help me tackle problems I wouldn't even know how to approach on my own.

At the moment, I'm mainly using **Codex** and **Claude Code** to assist with development, and they've been incredibly helpful so far.

Any advice, personal experiences, recommended resources, or reality checks would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks! 🚀🎮

comments.author: korypostma
comments.body:
I'll summarize what could be a very long book into a few things:
1. Use the 90/10 engineering principal.  Do 90% of the work with 10% effort.  Save that last 10% of the work for when you have 90% effort available.  This is like saying prototype first, polish later.
2. Godot with GDExtensions, I have used UE4/UE5 and Unity, as well, in the past.
3. Full game prototype, make sure it is fun.  Let people close to you play it, they won't always be honest to not hurt your feelings.  Find unbiased people online to test it and provide constructive feedback.
4. Beginners waste too much time on details that don't matter right now.  Focus on the code and gameplay loop, polish comes later.  Plan first before implementing.

comments.author: TheReviewerWildTake
comments.body:
There are good gamedev videos on the internet about principles and foundations that still fully apply to AI assisted work.

The main thing to be prepared with AI specifically, is to prevent your project from becoming bloated and hard to understand\\maintain. (this is one of the reason why AI games often just die as unfinished demo projects)  
  
It is fine if AI knows better how to work with library that does something very useful, but you don\`t want just to generate everything as a "black box", you want to have clarity about foundation you are creating, and clarity about why something gets plugged in, what it does, why this and not that etc.

This is why it is usually helpful to start from super basic structure that allows you to fully grasp concepts you are using, classes you are creating.  
  
My initial foundation is just an easy to read\\easy to refactor setup where things are just dots and rectangles on whatever "canvas" I am using.    
This allows to keep clear structure where I can see core concepts and see how they grow in complexity, without losing track of what is doing what.  
So I see classes like player, enemy, world (or board) generation, restart, score, inventory etc.  
I may not always know what method X is doing on the low level, but I want to know how it is limiting me etc.

So maybe my knowledge of whatever language is not 100% and I can\`t fully comprehend every library, but I am trying to understand what is going on in structural way.  
Like I really want to keep track on the connection of my "restart button" to enemy generation class, and how it is packed with a method used for randomized equipment, and how that randomized equipment is stored in third file, etc.

Because when time comes to change something or expand, I don\`t have to hope for the best and rely on AI not losing context, I know that I can scope my problem, because I keep track of how things connect to each other in the code.  
This also makes sure that I know what is possible to do without big reworks, and what would affect whole bunch of concepts.  
AI can easily push you into overengineering things, which often becomes hard to read or impossible to track, because so many things are generated so quickly, without giving you chance to become familiar with codebase (as you just don\`t spend enough time reading it).   
  
Non-AI coder of the past would easily remember how his player character stores data, or what kind of data is accessible to the methods tied to the character.  
But AI can create situation, when it is very hard to read and understand what is going on, and how to narrow things down. Leaving you confused and dependent of AI even more and more. Because you don\`t understand what happens where, what are existing dependencies etc.  
  
So people constantly get into situations, where it is just way too much troubles to clean after AI, when you hit certain levels of messiness\\complexity.  
And then they drop their unfinished game as fixing things sometimes can be much harder than building another demo.

comments.author: Ill-Past4609
comments.body: What I do and still currently doing, create a GDD. Start with the core loop expand out who cares if you are using placeholders for art. Create in phases test fix repeat.  Sometimes I have an idea and don’t want to create a new GDD so I ask codex in /plan my idea and codex gives me a full GDD with only that specific idea

comments.author: Ok-Object7409
comments.body:
* you're not at the stage to worry about this

* Godot might be the simplest. I'd suggest Unity since it has more tools and is more in-line with industry plus has good documentation and tutorials.

* Yes. Don't start Rimworld after a few small simple things.

* Not willing to fail


Don't use AI. You're in the process of learning, not producing. AI is not a great learning tool even if used as one. That's why you should start with small simple projects.
